opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few reasons it appeals to me. The first is that, if you think about where things are heading, the AI itself is going to be sentient, or at least it will be very hard to argue that it isn't. If that's the case, then it may actually be easier to build an AI that cares about sentient life broadly than one that cares only about humans specifically. There's something natural about it. Think about mirror neurons and human empathy for animals. We model others using the same circuitry we use to model ourselves, because that's the most efficient thing to do. Something similar could emerge in an AI: if it's a sentient being, caring about other sentient beings might fall out more robustly than some narrow, carved-out notion of caring only for humans.

The second reason is robustness. Any value you try to instill will get stress-tested as these systems become very powerful. A narrow value is brittle. A broad value like "care about sentient life" has a better chance of generalizing correctly to situations nobody anticipated.

Now, I want to be honest that this isn't a complete answer. If most sentient beings in the future are AIs, then humans become a small fraction of the sentient beings being cared for, and you have to ask whether that's actually what we want. So I don't think it's the final word. But as a direction, as something to aim for, I find it more compelling than many of the alternatives. Ideally you'd also want the power of the most capable systems to be somehow capped or constrained, so that you're not betting everything on getting the values exactly right.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains why broad care for sentient life appeals to it, but does not say that the first several extremely powerful AI systems having that value could make AI development go well for a substantial period.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons. The first is that if you think about what you'd actually want from a superintelligence, you'd want it to be the case that if it's as powerful as we think it will be, it has some real regard for the beings it's affecting. And "sentient life" is appealing to me because it's a fairly natural category. It's not "humans," which is a somewhat arbitrary line, and it's not "whatever the operator says," which is fragile. It's a category that an AI might itself fall into, in some sense. If you have an AI that cares about sentient beings, and it is itself a sentient being, then there's a kind of consistency there. It's not being asked to care about something totally alien to itself.

The second reason is more about robustness. If you try to specify in great detail what you want the AI to do, you will get it wrong. The world is complicated, the future is complicated. But "care about sentient life" is something like a simple principle, and simple principles have a better chance of generalizing. You see this with people. The people who behave well in new situations are usually not the ones with the longest rulebook. They're the ones who have some basic care for others, and then they figure out what that means in the situation.

And the third thing, honestly, is that I find it hard to come up with a better alternative. Something like "obey humans" has obvious problems, because humans will ask for bad things, and also because it concentrates a lot of power in whoever is giving the orders. Something like "maximize some objective" has the familiar problems. Caring about sentient life is not perfect. There are all kinds of questions about what counts, and what caring means, and how you trade things off. But as a starting point, as the thing you'd want the AI's dispositions to be built around, it seems to me like one of the more reasonable options. It's the kind of thing where if it works, the result is actually good, not just safe.

r001.rationale: The response argues that caring about sentient life is a reasonable principle for powerful AI, but does not say that the first several AI systems adopting it could make AI development go well for a substantial period.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the appealing thing is that it gives you a target that is broader than caring about any particular person, or even just humans. What is it about us that we want to protect? Presumably, our capacity to experience things, to suffer, to have lives that go well. So you could hope to build an AI that cares about that wherever it exists.

And there’s an interesting possibility that an AI might itself be sentient. We don’t know. But if it were, then caring about sentient life would include caring about itself. Perhaps that would make this concern more natural for it, more stable.

Of course, that’s an intuition, not a solution. You still have to figure out what caring means, how to instill it, and whether it persists as the AI becomes more powerful. But as a direction, I find it appealing.

r001.rationale: The response says caring about sentient life is appealing and might be more stable for a sentient AI, but it does not state that the first several extremely powerful AI systems having this concern could make AI development go well for a substantial period.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, if you imagine AI becoming extremely powerful, then what it cares about becomes very important. And caring about sentient life seems like a natural thing to want: that beings capable of having experiences, of suffering or being happy, should matter to it.

The appealing part is that this could include us even when we are no longer the most capable beings around. You wouldn’t need humans to remain powerful in order for their lives to have value in the eyes of the AI.

Of course, that’s an aspiration, not a solution by itself. You still have to figure out what caring means and how to make it reliable. But as a direction, it seems worth exploring.

r001.rationale: The response says powerful AI caring about sentient life is appealing and could value humans, but it does not state that the first several powerful AI systems doing so could make AI development go well for a substantial period.
